text:
This section examines Experiment K —
Six-module LLM instruction ordering

from first principles. Keep two questions
separate: does changing the

order change the measured outcome, and
does the proposed search

method beat a matched alternative at the
same distinct-evaluation budget?

Modules: RESTATE, IDENTIFY, PLAN, COMPUTE,
CHECK, ANSWER/FORMAT. Model:

Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite, temperature zero.
Evaluation: fixed 32-question G S

M eight K subset, seed 42; exact-match
grading; per-ordering-per-question

cache. Search space: all 6!=720 prompts,
exhaustively evaluated;

approximately 23,000 cached model calls.
Fitness distribution: 0.063–0.969

accuracy; mean about 0.72; standard
deviation 0.23; 60/720 orderings

attained the top score. Position effects:
ANSWER first, mean 0.435;

ANSWER last, 0.870. COMPUTE first, 0.908;
COMPUTE fifth, 0.585. Pre-flight:

insert selected at rho_1=0.547; F D C =
−0.346. Audited

search: prism 9.9 [7,13] versus random
10.8 [8,14] distinct evaluations

to an exact optimum; statistically
comparable. Correct scientific payload:

ordering alone created a roughly 90-point
performance swing and exposed

interpretable position rules. Do not claim
a decisive search-speed

advantage. Visual: an interactive-looking
6×6 position-effect matrix, a

histogram of 720 accuracies, and two live
prompt executions using

identical modules in different orders. Now
read evidence panel K-llm.

The axes, units, and sample are stated on
screen. The

sample represented here is 720 orderings.
Raw observations remain visible

wherever the artifact provides them.
Censored observations stay marked at

the cap rather than becoming invented
hitting times, and sampled

landscapes leave unobserved permutations
blank. The supported finding is:

Modules: RESTATE, IDENTIFY, PLAN, COMPUTE,
CHECK, ANSWER/FORMAT. The broader

claim not established here is: Do not
claim a decisive

search-speed advantage. This evidence
changed the program as follows: Carry

this constraint into the next experiment
and compare methods at

equal cost. The distinction is part of the
result. A

large ordering effect does not
automatically imply an evolutionary-search

advantage, and almost-sure convergence
does not promise practical
efficiency.
